passage:
Age ten: Ishita and Bidisha called each other "Professor Pencil" and "Captain Crumbs" and doubled over laughing. Then a third girl joined in and joked about the way Bidisha stammered on a word. Bidisha went quiet and stared at her shoes. Ishita stopped laughing, walked over and said, "Sorry, that wasn't okay. Are you all right?"

Age fifteen: Anand's school trip was cancelled because of rain. "Great, just great," he said flatly, tapping his pen. His friend Ishita looked up from her phone and asked, "Are you joking, or actually upset?" Anand exhaled. "Upset. I'd saved up for it."

Age twenty-four: Bidisha joined a team overseas and cracked a dry joke about her own hopeless cooking. Two colleagues smiled politely; one looked puzzled. She noticed the silence, gently added, "That was meant to be funny, not a complaint," and afterwards kept to lighter, kinder jokes until she knew the group better.

qa.q: What did Ishita say to Bidisha after the third girl joked about the stammer?
qa.a: Ishita said, "Sorry, that wasn't okay. Are you all right?"

qa.q: How do the three scenes show humour being read differently as people grow up?
qa.a: At ten a joke turns hurtful when Bidisha goes quiet, at fifteen sarcasm hides real upset until Ishita asks whether Anand is joking, and at twenty-four Bidisha finds that a dry joke travels badly to a new team and watches reactions before joking again.

qa.q: What was Anand probably feeling when he said, "Great, just great"?
qa.a: Anand was disappointed and frustrated about the cancelled trip, and his flat voice covered how upset he really was.

qa.q: What did Bidisha do well when her joke met a polite silence?
qa.a: She noticed the reaction, clarified her intent gently, and switched to lighter jokes until she knew the group.

grounding: Humour that can be friendly or hurtful, sarcastic or sincere, and culturally variable, seen at three ages with check-ins on how others react.
